claim: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) has spread explosively in the last 20 years along with its mosquito vector.
source: Along with its mosquito vector, the Alphavirus chikungunya virus (CHIKV) has spread explosively in the last 20 years, and there is no approved treatment for chikungunya fever.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiological spread of CHIKV, presented as established fact in the abstract.

claim: There is no approved treatment for chikungunya fever.
source: Along with its mosquito vector, the Alphavirus chikungunya virus (CHIKV) has spread explosively in the last 20 years, and there is no approved treatment for chikungunya fever.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the current state of medical treatments.

claim: CHIKV generates dedicated organelles for viral RNA replication on the plasma membrane of the infected cell, called spherules.
source: On the plasma membrane of the infected cell, CHIKV generates dedicated organelles for viral RNA replication, so-called spherules.
evidence: This is a statement about the cellular location and function of spherules, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The architecture of the full CHIKV spherule organelle is unknown.
source: Whereas structures exist for several viral proteins that make up the spherule, the architecture of the full organelle is unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The viral protein nsP1 serves as a base for the assembly of a larger protein complex at the neck of the membrane bud.
source: This reveals that the viral protein nsP1 serves as a base for the assembly of a larger protein complex at the neck of the membrane bud.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-electron tomography data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The viral helicase-protease nsP2 has no membrane affinity on its own.
source: Biochemical assays show that the viral helicase-protease nsP2, while having no membrane affinity on its own, is recruited to membranes by nsP1.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: NsP2 is recruited to membranes by nsP1.
source: Biochemical assays show that the viral helicase-protease nsP2, while having no membrane affinity on its own, is recruited to membranes by nsP1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-pelletation assays in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Full-sized spherules contain a single copy of the viral genome in double-stranded form.
source: The tomograms further reveal that full-sized spherules contain a single copy of the viral genome in double-stranded form.
evidence: This is based on filament tracing analysis of cryo-electron tomograms shown in Figure 4.

claim: The energy released by RNA polymerization is sufficient to remodel the membrane to the characteristic spherule shape.
source: The energy released by RNA polymerization is found to be sufficient to remodel the membrane to the characteristic spherule shape.
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chikungunya is characterized by rapid onset of fever followed by debilitating joint pains and arthritis that can last for months or years.
source: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne disease characterized by a rapid onset of fever, followed by debilitating joint pains and arthritis that can last for months or years (Weaver and Lecuit, 2015; Burt et al., 2017).
evidence: This clinical description is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Suspected chikungunya cases have surpassed 500,000 per year in several recent years.
source: It is severely underdiagnosed, but suspected cases have surpassed 500,000/year in several recent years (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chikungunya).
evidence: This epidemiological data is cited from WHO fact sheets.

claim: CHIKV is a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the Alphavirus genus (family Togaviridae).
source: The causative agent of chikungunya is chikungunya virus (CHIKV), a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the Alphavirus genus (family Togaviridae).
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification based on established virology knowledge.

claim: CHIKV has adapted to a new mosquito host, Aedes albopictus, which inhabits more temperate regions.
source: One reason for this is its adaptation to a new mosquito host, Aedes albopictus, which inhabits more temperate regions (Tsetsarkin et al., 2007; Vazeille et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on CHIKV adaptation.

claim: There are no approved vaccines or antivirals against any Alphavirus-caused diseases.
source: There are no approved vaccines or antivirals against any Alphavirus-caused diseases.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the current state of medical interventions.

claim: The Alphavirus replication organelle is formed as an outward-facing plasma membrane bud with a diameter of 50–80 nm.
source: This organelle is formed as an outward-facing plasma membrane bud with a diameter of 50–80 nm (Ahola et al., 2021).
evidence: This structural description is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The size of the membrane bud has been shown to depend on the length of the viral genome.
source: The size of the membrane bud has been shown to depend on the length of the viral genome (Kallio et al., 2013).
evidence: This relationship is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The spherule bud is thought to have a stable, open neck that connects it to the cytoplasm.
source: The bud is thought to have a stable, open neck that connects it to the cytoplasm, and this high-curvature membrane shape persists for several hours in the infected cell during active RNA production.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis or model based on existing knowledge.

claim: The Alphavirus genome codes for four non-structural proteins (nsP1–nsP4).
source: The Alphavirus genome codes for four non-structural proteins (nsP1–nsP4), initially produced as one polyprotein, with distinct functions in the viral genome replication (Ahola et al., 2021; Rupp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a basic fact about Alphavirus molecular biology supported by citations.

claim: NsP1 caps the 5' end of the new viral RNA independently of the host-cell capping machinery.
source: NsP1 caps the 5' end of the new viral RNA independently of the host-cell capping machinery (Ahola et al., 2021).
evidence: This functional description is supported by a citation.

claim: NsP1 is the only nsP reported to bind membranes.
source: It is the only nsP reported to bind membranes, and its membrane affinity is enhanced by, but not dependent on, a palmitoylation site (Ahola et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: NsP1's membrane affinity is enhanced by, but not dependent on, a palmitoylation site.
source: It is the only nsP reported to bind membranes, and its membrane affinity is enhanced by, but not dependent on, a palmitoylation site (Ahola et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: NsP2 has RNA helicase and RNA triphosphatase activity in its N-terminal domain.
source: NsP2 has RNA helicase and RNA triphosphatase activity in its N-terminal domain, and its C-terminus harbors a cysteine protease domain which cleaves the polyprotein into individual nsPs.
evidence: This is a description of nsP2's enzymatic activities based on established knowledge.

claim: NsP2's C-terminus harbors a cysteine protease domain which cleaves the polyprotein into individual nsPs.
source: NsP2 has RNA helicase and RNA triphosphatase activity in its N-terminal domain, and its C-terminus harbors a cysteine protease domain which cleaves the polyprotein into individual nsPs.
evidence: This is a description of nsP2's protease function based on established knowledge.

claim: NsP3 has ADP-ribosyl hydrolase activity and interacts with several host-cell proteins.
source: NsP3 has ADP-ribosyl hydrolase activity and interacts with several host-cell proteins (Götte et al., 2018).
evidence: This functional description is supported by a citation.

claim: NsP4 is the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase directly responsible for the production of new viral RNA.
source: NsP4 is the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase directly responsible for the production of new viral RNA.
evidence: This is a basic fact about nsP4's function based on established knowledge.

claim: When overexpressed in eukaryotic systems and gently extracted from the plasma membrane, nsP1 forms a ring-shaped dodecamer.
source: When overexpressed in eukaryotic systems and gently extracted from the plasma membrane, nsP1 was shown to form a ring-shaped dodecamer, displaying its active sites to the inside of the ring and the membrane-binding surfaces to the outside.
evidence: This structural observation is based on published structures cited in the text (Jones et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).

claim: The nsP1 dodecamer displays its active sites to the inside of the ring and the membrane-binding surfaces to the outside.
source: When overexpressed in eukaryotic systems and gently extracted from the plasma membrane, nsP1 was shown to form a ring-shaped dodecamer, displaying its active sites to the inside of the ring and the membrane-binding surfaces to the outside.
evidence: This structural description is based on published structures.

claim: It was suggested that the nsP1 dodecamer may bind at and stabilize the high-curvature membrane neck.
source: It was thus suggested that the nsP1 dodecamer may bind at and stabilize the high-curvature membrane neck.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis from previous work.

claim: Cryo-electron tomograms of the peripheral plasma membrane occasionally showed CHIKV spherules appearing as clusters of balloon-shaped organelles sitting at the plasma membrane.
source: Cryo-electron tomograms of the peripheral plasma membrane occasionally showed CHIKV spherules appearing as clusters of balloon-shaped organelles sitting at the plasma membrane (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—videos 1; 2).
evidence: This observation is directly supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CHIKV spherules have a diameter ranging from 50 to 70 nm.
source: They had a diameter ranging from 50 to 70 nm, consistent with what has been reported from resin-section EM (Kujala et al., 2001).
evidence: This measurement is supported by both the current data and a citation to previous EM studies.

claim: Cryo-electron tomograms revealed filamentous densities coiled on the inside of the membrane buds.
source: In addition to the membrane topology, the cryo-electron tomograms also revealed filamentous densities coiled on the inside of the membrane buds (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This observation is directly shown in the tomograms in Figure 1.

claim: The filaments inside spherules are likely viral RNA, possibly in its dsRNA replicative intermediate form.
source: The position and width of the filaments make it likely that they are viral RNA, possibly in its dsRNA replicative intermediate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed properties of the filaments.

claim: In all imaged spherules, a macromolecular complex was observed sitting at the membrane neck.
source: On the other hand, in all imaged spherules, we observed a macromolecular complex sitting at the membrane neck (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is a consistent observation across all spherules examined in the tomograms.

claim: In well-resolved individual spherules, the neck complex appeared to be bipartite with a base pinching the neck and a second part protruding toward the cytoplasm.
source: In well-resolved individual spherules, the complex seemed to be bipartite with a base pinching the neck of the spherule and a second part protruding toward the cytoplasm of the cell (Figure 1C).
evidence: This structural observation is based on high-resolution tomograms shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A 34 Å subtomogram average was calculated from 64 spherules without imposing any symmetry.
source: A 34 Å subtomogram average was calculated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) from 64 spherules without imposing any symmetry.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method and its result.

claim: The subtomogram average revealed that the neck complex is composed of two parts: a membrane-bound 'base' and a barrel-like 'crown'.
source: It revealed that the complex is composed of two parts: a membrane-bound 'base' and a barrel-like 'crown' (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This structural description is based on the subtomogram average shown in Figure 2.

claim: The base of the neck complex fits the membrane neck snugly.
source: The base fits the membrane neck snugly (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This observation is shown in the subtomogram average in Figure 2.

claim: The crown is composed of three rings and protrudes toward the cytoplasm.
source: The crown is composed of three rings and protrudes toward the cytoplasm (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This structural feature is visible in the subtomogram average in Figure 2.

claim: At the current resolution, there is no visible connection between the base and the crown.
source: At the current resolution, there is no visible connection between the base and the crown.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current structural data.

claim: A third component of the neck complex is a central density protruding from the base, through the crown toward the cytoplasm.
source: A third component of the neck complex is a central density protruding from the base, through the crown toward the cytoplasm.
evidence: This structural feature is observed in the subtomogram average.

claim: The isolated nsP1 structure has a similar dimension to the base of the neck complex.
source: The recent structures of nsP1 revealed a ring-shaped dodecamer with a similar dimension to the base of the neck complex (Jones et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This comparison is based on published structures and the current subtomogram average.

claim: An overlay of the isolated nsP1 structure and the base of the neck complex showed a close match in size and shape.
source: An overlay of these two showed a close match in size and shape of the isolated nsP1 and the base of the neck complex (Figure 2I).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The best fit of nsP1 into the neck complex is such that the narrow side of the nsP1 ring, carrying the membrane-association sites, is in direct contact with the membrane.
source: The best fit of nsP1 into the neck complex is such that the narrow side of the nsP1 ring, carrying the membrane-association sites, is in direct contact with the membrane.
evidence: This is based on fitting the published nsP1 structure into the subtomogram average.

claim: There may be additional densities bound to the inside of the nsP1 ring in the full-neck complex as compared to the heterologously expressed nsP1.
source: This overlay indicated that there may be additional densities bound to the inside of the nsP1 ring in the full-neck complex as compared to the heterologously expressed nsP1.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the structures.

claim: Based on the volume of the crown and teeth (1500–1700 nm3), their molecular mass is estimated to be 1.2–1.4 MDa.
source: However, based on their volume of 1500–1700 nm3, we estimate them to have a molecular mass of 1.2–1.4 MDa.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured volume from the subtomogram average.

claim: The rod-like density at the center of the neck complex extending out from nsP1 through the crown is the only candidate to be the new viral RNA leaving the spherule.
source: At the center of the neck complex, extending out from nsP1 through the crown is a rod-like density that is the only candidate to be the new viral RNA leaving the spherule.
evidence: This is an inference based on the position and properties of the observed density.

claim: Monomeric nsP1 did not bind appreciably to vesicles in the absence of any negatively charged lipids.
source: In the absence of any negatively charged lipids, nsP1 did not bind appreciably to the vesicles (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MLV pulldown assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NsP1 has concentration-dependent binding to PS-containing membranes.
source: This revealed that nsP1 has concentration-dependent binding to PS-containing membranes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MLV pulldown assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NsP1 showed very similar, concentration-dependent binding to PG- and PI-containing membranes.
source: NsP1 showed very similar, concentration-dependent binding to PG- and PI-containing membranes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MLV pulldown assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NsP1 had a higher affinity to membranes containing low PIP concentrations and almost no affinity for membranes with higher concentration of these lipids.
source: Curiously, nsP1 had a higher affinity to membranes containing low PIP concentrations and almost no affinity for membranes with higher concentration of these lipids (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MLV pulldown assays shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: For each PIP, nsP1 showed weaker membrane association than to membranes containing monovalent anionic lipids.
source: For each PIP, we observed weaker membrane association than to membranes containing monovalent anionic lipids (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This comparison is based on the MLV pulldown assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: No accumulation of fluorescent nsP1 was seen on GUVs consisting of phosphatidyl choline and cholesterol.
source: No accumulation of fluorescent nsP1 was seen on GUVs consisting of phosphatidyl choline and cholesterol (a net-uncharged membrane).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The equivalent charge density introduced in the form of either 20% PS or 5% PI(4,5)P2 led to visible binding of nsP1 to the surface of GUVs.
source: On the other hand, the equivalent charge density introduced in the form of either 20% PS or 5% PI(4,5)P2 led to visible binding of nsP1 to the surface of GUVs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 20% of the PI(4,5)P2-containing GUVs were positive for nsP1 binding, whereas 50% of PS-containing GUVs were positive.
source: 20% of the PI(4,5)P2-containing GUVs were positive for nsP1 binding, whereas 50% of PS-containing GUVs were positive, paralleling the MLV pulldown results (Figure 3E).
evidence: This quantification is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NsP2 had no affinity to membranes containing 70% PS.
source: In the pulldown assay, nsP2 had no affinity to membranes containing 70% PS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-pelletation assay shown in Figure 3F.

claim: NsP2 was recruited to the membrane by nsP1 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: However, nsP2 was recruited to the membrane by nsP1 in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-pelletation assay shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The filaments in the spherule lumen were frequently observed to be relatively straight over a large fraction of the spherule lumen.
source: The filaments were frequently observed to be relatively straight over a large fraction of the spherule lumen, which is more compatible with the persistence length of dsRNA (63 nm) than that of single-stranded RNA (1 nm) (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 1; Abels et al., 2005; Hyeon et al., 2006).
evidence: This observation is based on the tomograms and is compared to known persistence lengths from the literature.

claim: The persistence length of dsRNA is 63 nm.
source: The filaments were frequently observed to be relatively straight over a large fraction of the spherule lumen, which is more compatible with the persistence length of dsRNA (63 nm) than that of single-stranded RNA (1 nm) (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 1; Abels et al., 2005; Hyeon et al., 2006).
evidence: This value is cited from published literature.

claim: The persistence length of single-stranded RNA is 1 nm.
source: The filaments were frequently observed to be relatively straight over a large fraction of the spherule lumen, which is more compatible with the persistence length of dsRNA (63 nm) than that of single-stranded RNA (1 nm) (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 1; Abels et al., 2005; Hyeon et al., 2006).
evidence: This value is cited from published literature.

claim: The total length of filaments was 18,600±2900 Å/spherule in the first dataset and 21,400±1600 Å/spherule in the second dataset.
source: The total length of filaments for each dataset were 18,600±2900 Å/spherule and 21,400±1600 Å/spherule (Figure 4B).
evidence: This measurement is based on automated filament tracing of tomograms shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The distance between two base pairs in A-form dsRNA is 2.56 Å.
source: Assuming that the RNA was double-stranded and adopted an A conformation, the distance between two base pairs is 2.56 Å (Hardison and Chu, 2021; Tolokh et al., 2014).
evidence: This structural parameter is cited from published literature.

claim: The filament length corresponds to 7300±1150 and 8400±600 bp/spherule in the two tomograms, respectively.
source: Based on that assumption, the filament length corresponds to 7300±1150 and 8400±600 bp/spherule in the two tomograms, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured filament lengths assuming A-form dsRNA.

claim: The measured RNA length corresponds to an average ~80–90% of a single replicon RNA copy at 8820 bp.
source: This corresponds to an average ~80–90% of a single replicon RNA copy at 8820 bp.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the measured RNA length to the known replicon size.

claim: All spherules contain exactly one full-length copy of the template strand, of which a high but variable fraction is present in the dsRNA form.
source: It thus seems parsimonious to assume that all spherules, in fact, contain exactly one full-length copy of the template strand, of which a high but variable fraction is present in the dsRNA form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA length measurements.

claim: With a bending rigidity of κ=10 kBT, the membrane tension is σ=10–5 N/m, within the range of experimentally measured membrane tensions.
source: For comparison, with a bending rigidity of κ=10 kBT, we obtain σ=10–5 N/m, within the range of experimentally measured membrane tensions (Baumgart et al., 2003; Roux et al., 2005).
evidence: This is calculated from the model and compared to literature values.

claim: Spherules at different stages in the growth process corresponding to each of the predicted membrane shapes were observed in cryo-electron tomograms of cells transduced with SFV replicon particles.
source: Notably, we were able to observe spherules at different stages in the growth process corresponding to each of the predicted membrane shapes, in cryo-electron tomograms of cells transduced with replicon particles from the Alphavirus SFV, a close relative of CHIKV (Figure 4D, lower half).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 4D comparing predicted and observed shapes.

claim: An energy barrier of roughly 250 kcal/mol has to be overcome going from a flat membrane to a fully formed spherule.
source: With a bending rigidity of κ=10 kBT, we find by solving Equation 1 that an energy barrier of roughly 250 kcal/mol has to be overcome going form a flat membrane to a fully formed spherule (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The free energy released by RNA polymerization is around 10 times larger than the energy required to bend the membrane, even at its peak 'resistance.'
source: Comparing the two, we conclude that the free energy released by RNA polymerization is around 10 times larger than the energy required to bend the membrane, even at its peak 'resistance.'
evidence: This comparison is based on the calculated energy requirements and known polymerization energetics.

claim: RNA polymerization is sufficient to remodel the spherule membrane into its characteristic shape, assuming the neck geometry is constrained.
source: Thus, RNA polymerization is sufficient to remodel the spherule membrane into its characteristic shape, assuming the neck geometry is constrained.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mathematical modeling and energy calculations.

claim: Alphaviruses are not only a major source of morbidity, but their unique RNA replication mechanism is also used to develop self-replicating RNA vaccines that induce a more potent immune response than conventional mRNA vaccines.
source: Alphaviruses are not only a major source of morbidity, but their unique RNA replication mechanism is also used to develop self-replicating RNA vaccines that induce a more potent immune response than conventional mRNA vaccines (Ballesteros-Briones et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement about vaccine applications is supported by a citation.

claim: All positive-sense RNA viruses utilize cytoplasmic membranes to compartmentalize their RNA replication machineries.
source: All positive-sense RNA viruses utilize cytoplasmic membranes to compartmentalize their RNA replication machineries.
evidence: This is a general statement about positive-sense RNA viruses based on established knowledge.

claim: Replication compartments can be split into two groups based on membrane topology: double-membrane vesicles and membrane buds.
source: It has been suggested to split the replication compartments into two groups based on membrane topology: double-membrane vesicles and membrane buds.
evidence: This classification is presented as an established concept in the field.

claim: This grouping based on membrane topology has recently been shown to correlate with the newly proposed phyla Pisuviricota and Kitrinoviricota, respectively.
source: This grouping based on membrane topology has recently been shown to correlate with the newly proposed phyla Pisuviricota and Kitrinoviricota, respectively (Ahola and Racaniello, 2019).
evidence: This correlation is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Alphavirus spherules fall into the Kitrinoviricota category together with Flaviviruses and Nodaviruses.
source: Alphavirus spherules fall into the Kitrinoviricota category together with, e.g., Flaviviruses and Nodaviruses.
evidence: This taxonomic classification is based on established viral taxonomy.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography has revealed that Nodaviruses have a neck complex of similar dimensions as the Alphavirus neck complex.
source: Whereas nothing is yet known about any Flavivirus neck complex, cryo-electron tomography has revealed that Nodaviruses have a neck complex of similar dimensions as the Alphavirus neck complex that we present here (Unchwaniwala et al., 2021; Unchwaniwala et al., 2020).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to published cryo-ET studies.

claim: The double-membrane vesicles-type replication organelles of Coronaviruses have a neck complex connecting their lumen with the cytosol.
source: The double-membrane vesicles-type replication organelles of Coronaviruses indeed have a neck complex connecting their lumen with the cytosol (Wolff et al., 2020).
evidence: This structural feature is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The similarly shaped enteroviruses organelles are of autophagic origin, frequently open, and appear to lack a neck complex.
source: On the other hand, the similarly shaped enteroviruses organelles are of autophagic origin, frequently open, and appear to lack a neck complex (Dahmane et al., 2022).
evidence: This structural description is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The localization of the polymerase nsP4 to the neck complex would be easy to reconcile with a strand-displacement mechanism that couples RNA polymerization to the extrusion of the displaced strand through the neck complex into the cytoplasm.
source: Conceptually, the localization of the polymerase nsP4 to the neck complex would be easy to reconcile with a strand-displacement mechanism that couples RNA polymerization to the extrusion of the displaced strand through the neck complex into the cytoplasm (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: Bud-type replication organelles from different Kitrinoviricota viruses all tend to have a similar diameter because they all contain genomes of ~8–12 kb, which at a given density would all occupy a similar volume.
source: This may also suggest an explanation for why bud-type replication organelles from different Kitrinoviricota viruses all tend to have a similar diameter; they all contain genomes of ~8–12 kb, which at a given density would all occupy a similar volume.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The mathematical model shows that the pressure exerted by the confined dsRNA and the restriction of the neck geometry are sufficient to generate and maintain the high-energy shape of the spherule membrane.
source: Our mathematical model, consistent with the tomographic data, shows that the pressure exerted by the confined dsRNA and the restriction of the neck geometry are sufficient to generate and maintain the high-energy shape of the spherule membrane.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model shows that the energy released by RNA polymerization is sufficient to drive the membrane shape remodeling.
source: Crucially, the model also shows that the energy released by RNA polymerization is sufficient to drive the membrane shape remodeling.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mathematical modeling and energy calculations.

claim: This establishes polymerase-driven budding as a new membrane remodeling mechanism.
source: This establishes polymerase-driven budding as a new membrane remodeling mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: Even though polymerase-driven budding does not require any lipids or proteins stabilizing the domed spherule membrane, it can still be assumed to lead to curvature-dependent sorting of membrane components through curvature-composition coupling.
source: Notably, even though polymerase-driven budding does not require any lipids or proteins stabilizing the domed spherule membrane, it can still be assumed to lead to curvature-dependent sorting of membrane components through curvature-composition coupling (Bashkirov et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to published work on membrane biophysics.

claim: This mechanism may explain data suggesting the presence of the host tetraspanin CD81 at CHIKV replication sites.
source: This may explain data suggesting the presence of the host tetraspanin CD81 at CHIKV replication sites (Lasswitz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for published observations.

claim: Semliki forest virus (SFV) nsP1 has been reported to associate with phosphatidyl serine (PS).
source: Semliki forest virus (SFV) nsP1 has been reported to associate with phosphatidyl serine (PS), an abundant lipid on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Ahola et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on SFV nsP1.

claim: PS is an abundant lipid on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: Semliki forest virus (SFV) nsP1 has been reported to associate with phosphatidyl serine (PS), an abundant lipid on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Ahola et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement of established cell biology knowledge.

claim: NsP1 primarily binds monovalent anionic lipids.
source: However, the in vitro reconstitution showed that nsP1 primarily binds monovalent anionic lipids (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MLV pulldown and GUV binding assays in Figure 3.

claim: Monovalent anionic lipids are reported to have near-zero or slightly positive spontaneous curvature.
source: Such lipids are reported to have near-zero or slightly positive spontaneous curvature, which excludes nsP1-induced lipid recruitment as a mechanism for stabilizing the spherule shape (Dymond, 2021).
evidence: This lipid property is cited from published literature.

claim: NsP1-induced lipid recruitment is excluded as a mechanism for stabilizing the spherule shape.
source: Such lipids are reported to have near-zero or slightly positive spontaneous curvature, which excludes nsP1-induced lipid recruitment as a mechanism for stabilizing the spherule shape (Dymond, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipid binding properties and known lipid curvature preferences.

claim: The initial positive strand may be present in a nascent spherule which grows as the single strand is turned into dsRNA.
source: This process may happen in two ways: (i) the initial positive strand is present in a nascent spherule which grows as the single strand is turned into dsRNA or (ii) the initial positive strand is translocated into the spherule lumen concomitant with the production of the complementary negative strand.
evidence: This is presented as one of two possible mechanisms for spherule formation.

claim: The initial positive strand may be translocated into the spherule lumen concomitant with the production of the complementary negative strand.
source: This process may happen in two ways: (i) the initial positive strand is present in a nascent spherule which grows as the single strand is turned into dsRNA or (ii) the initial positive strand is translocated into the spherule lumen concomitant with the production of the complementary negative strand.
evidence: This is presented as one of two possible mechanisms for spherule formation.

claim: Either mechanism (i) or (ii) for initial strand handling are compatible with the mathematical model described.
source: Either of (i) or (ii) are compatible with the model described below.
evidence: This is a statement about the flexibility of the mathematical model.

claim: The membrane is described as a thin elastic sheet in a Helfrich-type model.
source: We describe the membrane as a thin elastic sheet in a Helfrich-type model.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical modeling approach.

claim: The RNA is modeled as a semiflexible polymer that exerts a pressure onto the membrane.
source: The RNA, which is modeled as a semiflexible polymer, exerts a pressure onto the membrane that causes the spherule to expand.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical modeling approach.

claim: During spherule expansion, the neck complex keeps the membrane neck size constant.
source: During this process the neck complex keeps the membrane neck size constant.
evidence: This is an assumption in the mathematical model based on the structural observations.

claim: The VRP system results in a self-limiting single-cycle infection.
source: The VRPs, described previously, were kindly provided by Andres Merits, Tartu (Gläsker et al., 2013). Briefly, the system consists of a viral genomic RNA in which structural proteins were replaced by a fluorescent protein, and the helper RNAs C and E coding, respectively, for the capsid and the E3, E2, 6 K, E1 structural proteins.
evidence: This is a description of the VRP system used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: SFV-transduced cells were treated with the PI 3-kinase inhibitor Wortmannin at a final concentration of 100 nM to inhibit the endocytosis of plasma membrane-located spherules.
source: 1 hr after transduction, SFV-transduced cells were treated with the PI 3-kinase inhibitor Wortmannin (LC laboratories, Woburn, MA, USA) at a final concentration of 100 nM to inhibit the endocytosis of plasma membrane-located spherules (Spuul et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, with the rationale supported by a citation.

claim: The crown subcomplex has a volume of 1500–1700 nm3.
source: However, based on their volume of 1500–1700 nm3, we estimate them to have a molecular mass of 1.2–1.4 MDa.
evidence: This volume measurement is derived from the subtomogram average.

claim: The replicon RNA used in the VRPs is 8820 bp in length.
source: This corresponds to an average ~80–90% of a single replicon RNA copy at 8820 bp.
evidence: This is the known size of the replicon RNA used in the experiments.

claim: A dsRNA form of the filaments would be consistent with immunofluorescence observations of high loads of dsRNA at Alphavirus replication sites.
source: A dsRNA form of the filaments would also be consistent with immunofluorescence observations of high loads of dsRNA at Alphavirus replication sites (Spuul et al., 2011) and the positioning of the helicase nsP2 at the neck complex where it could serve a role in unwinding dsRNA (Figure 3F–H; Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This consistency is supported by citations to published immunofluorescence studies.

claim: The positioning of the helicase nsP2 at the neck complex is consistent with it serving a role in unwinding dsRNA.
source: A dsRNA form of the filaments would also be consistent with immunofluorescence observations of high loads of dsRNA at Alphavirus replication sites (Spuul et al., 2011) and the positioning of the helicase nsP2 at the neck complex where it could serve a role in unwinding dsRNA (Figure 3F–H; Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and known helicase function, supported by a citation.
